e.t: This Greek word means “boast”: to speak proudly about oneself, one’s abilities, or one’s accomplishments. It is a verb, so it describes the act of expressing such pride rather than naming a person or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only once, in Job 3:14. The word’s basic sense is therefore clear, while the precise force of that act in Job depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its use points to confident, self-exalting speech rather than a quiet inward feeling.

This word is a proper name referring to Azēka, also rendered Azika. It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it identifies a named location or designation in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs six times in six verses, from Joshua through Jeremiah, including passages associated with Joshua, Samuel, Chronicles, and Jeremiah. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical function is simply the name Azēka or Azika.

Akrabin, also rendered Akravin, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once each in Numbers, Joshua, and Judges. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise referent cannot be described further here; however, the supplied references show that it is used consistently as a name in these passages.

This word means “truly,” affirming that a statement or action is genuine, factual, or certain. It is an adverb, so it strengthens or qualifies what is being said rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 18 times, showing a recurring way to emphasize the truth of a statement. Its exact force in any verse is understood from the surrounding words and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “thresh”: to separate grain from its husks or stalks by beating or processing the harvested crop. It describes an agricultural action rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. The word occurs nine times across eight Old Testament verses in the Greek LXX, including passages from Deuteronomy, Judges, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Micah. In Scripture, threshing can be described as an ordinary farming task, while related imagery may portray forceful crushing; the precise force depends on the surrounding verse.

This word means “almond tree,” the tree that produces almonds. It is a noun naming a particular kind of tree rather than expressing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ecclesiastes 12:5. The word’s basic meaning remains botanical and specific; the surrounding passage is needed to understand any figurative or contextual significance attached to the almond tree there.

Andronikos is a personal name, also represented as Anthronikos. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, this name occurs five times, all in 2 Maccabees, covering references from 2 Maccabees 4:31 through 5:23. The precise role of the person named depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself functions as a proper name.

This adjective means “unlike” or “dissimilar,” describing someone or something that does not resemble another. It is a word of comparison: it points to a difference between two people, things, or qualities rather than naming the specific difference itself. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Wisdom 2:15. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what is being compared there, but the word’s basic sense remains a lack of likeness or resemblance.

This noun means “softness,” describing the quality of being soft rather than a person, action, or object itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: once in Deuteronomy and twice in Ezekiel. Its precise shade of meaning in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject, but the central idea remains softness. The word appears in Deuteronomy 28:56, Ezekiel 17:4, and Ezekiel 17:9.

This Greek LXX verb means “render” or “surrender”: to give something back, hand it over, or deliver what is owed or required. It can describe returning a person or thing, yielding something to another, or fulfilling an obligation. The word occurs 189 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, so its precise force depends on what is being given and to whom. Its broad use consistently centers on transferring something into another person’s hands or care.

This noun describes a condition of “loss of all sense”—the absence or collapse of ordinary understanding and judgment. It names a state rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs three times, in Sirach, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and its context.

e.h: Removing Something by Taking It Off
e.t: “Strip off” describes the action of removing an outer layer or surface from something. It is a verb, so it names an action rather than a person, object, or quality. This Greek Old Testament word appears three times, all in Leviticus 14. Its central meaning is the removal of something by taking it off. The precise object and force depend on the surrounding verse.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Apphous” or “Apfus.” It identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 2:5. Since the surrounding verse text is not included, the name itself establishes the person’s identification, while the passage supplies any further information about who that person was or why he is mentioned.

This noun refers to a juniper tree or cedar, a kind of tree named in the Greek Old Testament. Its basic meaning identifies the tree itself rather than an action, quality, or person. In the LXX, it occurs once, at Hosea 14:9. The precise significance of the tree in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word’s ordinary reference is a juniper or cedar tree.

This word means “artaba,” a noun used as the name of a specific term or measure. Its exact significance in a particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, since no verse text is available here. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice: once in Isaiah 5:10 and once in Bel and the Dragon 1:3. The word itself identifies the named unit rather than expressing an action, quality, or relationship.

This adjective means “without roof; unsheltered.” It describes someone or something lacking the protection of a roof or shelter. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, so its basic sense remains focused and concrete rather than broad or abstract. The word’s exact force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea is being exposed because shelter is absent.

Ater, also given as Atir, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears five times, all in Ezra and Nehemiah. Because it functions as a personal name, its meaning is identifying rather than descriptive: it points to a person named Ater. The name appears in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 and 10. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “contact,” referring to physical touching or coming into contact with something. It describes the point or act where one thing touches another, rather than an abstract relationship or general association. The word occurs 75 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, especially in Leviticus, where contact is repeatedly discussed in connection with bodily conditions and ritual assessment. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains direct physical contact.

Baladan is a proper name, also rendered Valathan. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 2 Kings 20:12. The name itself supplies identification, while the surrounding verse and passage provide the person’s role and significance in that account. Thus, its ordinary meaning is simply the personal name Baladan, not a general word with a broader definition.

This noun means “sole of the foot,” the underside or bottom surface of a person’s foot. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for the foot’s contact with the ground and for describing the lower part of something shaped like a foot. It occurs 70 times across 60 verses, chiefly in Exodus and other Old Testament books, showing a repeated physical meaning rather than an abstract idea.

This verb means to “scream” or “shout”—to raise the voice loudly and urgently. It describes an audible cry rather than a quiet thought or ordinary speech. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 153 times, showing that loud vocal expression is its normal sense across many settings. The precise force—whether a cry for help, a public summons, or an intense outburst—depends on the surrounding verse. Its listed range begins in Genesis and extends through the Epistle of Jeremiah.

This noun means “bone,” referring to the hard inner structure of the body. It names a physical part rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 9:13. Its basic meaning is therefore concrete and straightforward: a bone or bones of the body. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the word’s particular role there.

Gelampsour is a proper name, not a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named figure or place in the Greek Old Testament text, but the available lexical information does not specify which kind of name it is. The form appears only once, at 1 Samuel 27:8. It is also represented as Yelampsur, another spelling of the same name. Its precise referent must be identified from that verse’s surrounding text.

This noun means “earth” or “land.” It can refer broadly to the ground or the world people inhabit, or more specifically to a territory or region. The surrounding passage determines which sense is intended. This is a very common word in the Greek Old Testament and related writings, occurring 2,906 times, from Genesis through Song of Songs. Its range therefore includes both the physical earth and particular lands spoken of in Scripture.

This Greek LXX noun means “woman” or “wife,” referring to a female person and, according to context, to a woman in a marital relationship. It is used in both general references to women and specific references to wives, so the surrounding passage determines which sense is intended. The word occurs 838 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing broad use across these writings. Its earliest listed occurrence is Genesis 2:22, and its latest is Song of Songs 6:1.

Daphnē, also rendered Thafni, is a proper name. It identifies a named person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 4:33. The available information gives the name itself but not enough surrounding verse text to explain which individual or location bears it in that passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “prisoner,” referring to a person held in confinement or custody. It identifies someone whose freedom has been restricted by being detained. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in Genesis, Jeremiah, and Baruch. Its basic meaning remains the same whether it is rendered in the singular or plural. The surrounding passage determines who is imprisoned and why, but the word itself simply identifies the captive person.

This verb means “live through” or “pass,” describing continuing through a period or circumstance. It presents life as something a person goes through over time, rather than naming a separate object or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 21:21. The precise force of the verb in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is moving through life or a period and reaching its end.

This noun means “successor”: a person who follows another in an office, role, or position. It identifies someone who takes over after a predecessor, rather than simply describing any later person. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs seven times, including references in Chronicles, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. The precise person or position involved depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains one who comes after another and assumes that person’s place or responsibility.

This Greek LXX verb means “flash like lightening,” describing a sudden burst of bright movement or brilliance. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 16:22. Its basic sense is clear from the lexical definition, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is flashing and how the action functions there.

This Greek LXX noun means “difference” or “distinction”: a way of recognizing that one thing is not the same as another. It can refer to a separating feature, a contrast, or a discernible variety between things. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including Ezra, Wisdom, Sirach, and 1–2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what things the surrounding sentence compares or separates.

This noun means “righteous judge,” referring to a judge characterized by righteousness. It joins the ideas of judging and being righteous, identifying the person by the rightness associated with his judgment rather than merely by the act of deciding. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 12:41. That reference locates the word, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain its particular role there.

This noun means an “impious act”—an action showing disregard for God or what is holy. It names the deed itself rather than the person who commits it. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears once, in 2 Maccabees 12:3. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning points to conduct lacking reverence toward God.

This Greek LXX verb means “forsake.” It describes the act of abandoning someone or something rather than continuing to remain with it. In the available Greek Old Testament evidence, it occurs once, in Psalm 118:53. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s exact force in that verse must be understood from its sentence and context.

This Greek LXX verb means “spread on”: to apply something across a surface. It describes an action rather than an object, so the surrounding sentence identifies what is being applied and where. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Jeremiah 4:30. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, its exact object and force in that passage cannot be stated safely. Its basic sense remains the act of putting or spreading something onto another surface.

Ethi is a proper name, functioning as the personal name of an individual in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented as a general word describing an object, action, or quality, so its meaning is chiefly its identifying name rather than an expanded concept. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Ezra 9:1. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the person’s specific role or significance there.

This verb means to “cry out”—to call aloud in a noticeable or urgent way. It describes a spoken appeal or loud expression rather than a quiet thought. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 36 times, with many occurrences in Psalms, where people call out openly. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words and situation.

This word means “olive orchard,” referring to a cultivated place where olive trees grow. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament to name this kind of agricultural setting. The word occurs 16 times across 15 verses in the Greek Old Testament, including passages that mention land, trees, oil, and inherited possessions. Its basic meaning remains focused on an orchard or grove of olive trees rather than on the fruit or oil alone.

This word is a proper name: “Elthoula” or “Elthula.” It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament wording, rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at Joshua 19:4. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide an additional descriptive meaning for it there.

Emmor is a personal name rendered in English as “Emmor.” In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it identifies a named individual rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. It occurs 13 times across 12 verses, with twelve occurrences in Genesis and one in Judges. The references include Genesis 33:19 and several passages in Genesis 34, but verse meaning depends on the surrounding text.

gl: put the feet in bonds; fetter
d: put the feet in bonds; fetter

e.t: This verb means to put someone’s feet in bonds—to fetter or restrain them. It describes physically fastening a person so movement is prevented. In the LXX corpus, it occurs seven times, including passages from Judges, Ezra, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees. Its central idea remains the same wherever it appears: binding the feet and limiting a person’s ability to move freely.

This adjective describes a person who is bound by an oath, meaning that the person’s spoken commitment places them under an oath’s obligation. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented by this word, at Nehemiah 6:18, but the verse text is not included here. The central idea is oath-bound commitment; the surrounding passage determines how that commitment functions in the sentence.

“Able to accomplish” describes something capable of carrying a task through to completion or bringing an intended result about. As an adjective, the word characterizes a person, thing, or power by its effectiveness rather than merely by its willingness or intention. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 2:31. Without the surrounding verse text, the word itself gives the general idea of capability and successful execution, while the passage determines what specific task or result is in view.

This Greek LXX verb means “sing to,” describing vocal song directed toward someone. It expresses the act of singing to another person rather than simply making music without an indicated recipient. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Deuteronomy 18:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains the directed act of singing. It is therefore an action word focused on musical expression addressed to another.

This Greek LXX noun means “one who mounts.” It identifies a person in relation to mounting, rather than naming an action or object. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical material, including several occurrences in 2 Kings and single occurrences in Ezekiel, Job, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a person who mounts.

This verb means to add ornaments or decorate something further. It describes the act of making something more adorned or furnished with added beauty, rather than merely possessing an ornament. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ecclesiastes 1:15. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, but the word itself points to adding decoration or embellishment after something is already present.

“Shake at” is a verb describing an act of shaking something or someone toward or at a target. It presents movement directed at another person or object, rather than merely shaking without direction. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs five times, across four Old Testament verses and one deuterocanonical verse. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence.

This noun refers to an allowance of food or to a feast—a provision of food made available for eating. In the Greek Old Testament, it can describe either an ongoing food allotment or a substantial meal or celebration, depending on the surrounding sentence. The word occurs four times across three verses, in 2 Kings and Daniel. Its central idea is food provided for someone or food enjoyed together at a feast.

This adverb describes something done in a well-ordered or well-behaved manner. It points to conduct or activity that follows proper arrangement, discipline, or good order rather than confusion or disorder. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here: once in Proverbs and once in 3 Maccabees. Its basic sense concerns the manner in which something is carried out, while the surrounding verse determines what activity or conduct is being described.

This verb means “put to death.” It describes the act of causing someone to die, whether by a deliberate killing, a legal sentence, or another stated means. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, it occurs 152 times, so it commonly expresses the direct action of killing rather than merely the condition of being dead. Its precise force in any passage depends on who performs the action and why, but its central meaning remains the bringing of death upon a person.

Therma is a proper name rendered as “Therma.” It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at Joshua 16:6. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its precise identification cannot be explained further here; the available lexical evidence establishes the name itself and its single occurrence.

This Greek Old Testament word means “14; nun.” It is an indeclinable number, functioning as a fixed label rather than a word that changes its form in a sentence. The “14” identifies fourteen, while “nun” is included as the associated label in the word’s stated meaning. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Psalms 118:105. Its precise role there depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here.

Iermia is a proper name used in the Greek Old Testament, or Septuagint. As a name, it identifies someone in the text rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears seven times across seven verses, with occurrences in 1 Chronicles and Nehemiah. The supplied lexical meaning is simply “Iermia,” so no broader descriptive meaning should be attached to it without the surrounding verse and passage. This is a Greek LXX name and should remain distinct from similarly rendered names in other biblical language corpora.

This Greek LXX verb means “let down”: to lower or release something from a higher position. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament, across Exodus, Deuteronomy, Psalms, Isaiah, and Zechariah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being lowered or released in the surrounding passage.

This adverb means “abundantly,” describing something done or present in great abundance. It adds the idea of plentifulness or overflowing measure to the action or condition it modifies. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Zechariah 2:8, so its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage. Its basic meaning remains the clear sense of abundance rather than merely a small or ordinary amount.

This adjective describes someone or something as “tired” or “wearied.” It identifies a state of fatigue: the person or thing has become worn down, rather than naming an action such as tiring or exhausting. In the LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:14. Its exact force in that passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains a condition of weariness or tiredness.

This verb means to “outwit”—to defeat someone by using cleverness or superior strategy. It describes an intentional action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Exodus 1:10. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in that passage must be understood from its context. Its central idea remains clear: trying to gain an advantage over another through clever planning.

This verb means to bury something in the ground. It describes placing a person or object beneath the earth, with the action focused on burial rather than merely putting something nearby. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times, showing a recurring word for laying something underground. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being buried and the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains direct: to bury in the ground.

“Kitiaioi; Kitiei” is a proper name appearing in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named people or place, but the available wording does not provide enough context to specify which. The name occurs twice in the Greek LXX, once in Numbers 24:24 and once in Isaiah 23:1. Its precise reference in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This word refers to a “priestly garment.” It is an adjective used to describe clothing associated with priestly service. The central idea is not a person or an action, but a piece of clothing identified by its priestly use. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it appears once, in Ezra 2:69, so its meaning is narrowly attested there. Without the verse text, its basic lexical meaning can be stated confidently, while the garment’s exact significance in that passage depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX noun refers to an acquisition or possession—something obtained and held as one’s property. It can describe possessions generally rather than a particular kind of object. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, including passages from Job, Proverbs, Hosea, and Sirach. Its precise reference in any verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains something acquired, owned, or held.

Laisa is a proper name identifying a place in the Greek Old Testament. It is also rendered Lesa, but the supplied lexical definition gives these as the name’s forms rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. The name occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament: three times in Judges 18 and once in Isaiah 10. Its precise significance in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This word is a proper name: “Leuΐ” or “Lei,” referring to Levi. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used repeatedly as the name Levi, appearing 75 times across the corpus, especially in Numbers and 1 Chronicles. Its exact significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the personal name itself.

This noun means a calculator or a teacher of arithmetic. It refers to someone skilled in working with numbers and numerical calculations, rather than expressing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 26:15. The word’s central idea is practical numerical expertise: a person whose role involves calculating or teaching arithmetic. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the sentence uses the noun.

This verb means to revile or reproach—to address someone with insulting, abusive, or blaming words. It describes hostile speech directed against a person rather than a neutral disagreement. In the Greek LXX, it occurs nine times, chiefly in the Old Testament portion, and can describe people speaking against others in moments of conflict or complaint. The precise force in any verse depends on who is speaking and what has provoked the words, but the central idea remains verbal abuse or severe blame.

This word is a proper name rendered “Madai; Mathe.” It identifies a named person in the Greek Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or ordinary object. The name occurs twice in this corpus: once in Genesis 10:2 and once in 1 Chronicles 1:5. Since both occurrences are names in genealogical lists, the word’s main function is identification. Its precise significance in either passage comes from the surrounding genealogy, but the lexical meaning supplied here is the personal name itself.

This Greek LXX verb describes being softened and expresses cowardice. Its central idea is a loss of firmness or courage, whether understood as becoming soft or acting in a cowardly way. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Isaiah 53:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical range is limited to the ideas of being softened and cowardice.

This noun means “madness”: a condition or behavior marked by irrationality or loss of sound judgment. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it describes a recognizable state rather than a person’s name or a specific action. The word occurs six times across Psalms, Hosea, Wisdom, and 4 Maccabees, showing its use in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical contexts. Its precise force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse and speaker.

Machmas is a proper name for a place, also rendered Makhmas. It does not describe an action, quality, or ordinary object; it identifies a location named in the Greek Old Testament and in 1 Maccabees. The name occurs five times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in 1 Samuel, Ezra, Isaiah, Hosea, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its setting.

This Greek LXX noun means “blackness” and can refer to “a black cloud.” It describes a dark, cloudlike appearance rather than an action or person. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 19:26. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning is a dark or black appearance. This word should be understood as a Greek LXX term, distinct from Hebrew and Greek New Testament word entities.

This verb means “transfigure” or “apply.” It describes an action rather than a person or object, indicating that something is changed in form or put into use. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 9:22. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic sense centers on transfiguring or applying something.

This adjective means “stable”: something firm, settled, and able to remain in place. It describes a condition of steadiness rather than an action or event. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears twice, once in Genesis 49:26 and once in Jeremiah 38:17. Those references show that its basic sense is a quality of enduring firmness, while the surrounding verse determines what is stable in each case.

This verb means “mock”: to treat someone or something with contempt through ridicule or scorn. It describes an act of openly belittling rather than honoring or taking seriously. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 15 times, chiefly in the Old Testament portion of the LXX, including passages in Kings, Chronicles, Job, Psalms, and Proverbs. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains contemptuous ridicule.

“River” means a natural flowing watercourse. As a noun, this word refers to a river rather than to an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Jeremiah 38:40. It names a geographical feature in the landscape. That single occurrence supports this ordinary meaning, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain how the river functions in that passage. Its basic sense remains simply “river.”

This verb means to legislate: to make, establish, or give laws. It describes the act of setting binding rules or legal instructions for others to follow. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 11 times, including passages connected with God’s instruction and the giving of law. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains the authoritative establishment of laws or regulations.

This adjective means “mountainous,” describing land or a region marked by mountains or elevated terrain. It is used in the Greek Old Testament to identify places according to their rugged, hilly character rather than to name a person or action. The word occurs 11 times across 11 verses in the Greek Old Testament, appearing especially in Joshua, with additional occurrences in Genesis, Judges, and Proverbs. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding description of the land.

This word means “late”. It is an adverb that describes something happening at a later time, rather than early or promptly. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, in Genesis, Exodus, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its basic sense remains straightforward: it marks timing and points to something occurring late. The surrounding verse determines what action or event is being described, but the word itself contributes the idea of lateness. It does not name a person or object; it tells when something happens.

This adjective describes something extremely dreadful, terrible, or deeply frightening. It intensifies the seriousness of what it describes, presenting it as overwhelming rather than merely unpleasant or difficult. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either sentence depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea is clear: something fearsome, alarming, or exceptionally terrible.

This Greek LXX word means “all” or “every,” expressing the whole of a group, set, or amount rather than only part of it. It can function as a describing word, as in “every” person or thing, and it can also stand for the people or things included in the whole. It occurs 5,987 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing its broad use for complete scope or totality. Its precise force in a verse depends on what group or whole the surrounding sentence identifies.

This noun refers to going round or making a flank march—a movement that proceeds around rather than directly forward. It describes a route or maneuver, not a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Joshua 6:16. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense centers on moving around an opposing position or area. The related ideas of circling and approaching from the side are contained in the stated meaning itself.

“Of a shepherd” describes something associated with a shepherd or belonging to a shepherd’s work. As an adjective, it identifies a person, object, or role by its connection with shepherding. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs twice, once in 1 Samuel and once in Zechariah. The surrounding verse is needed to show exactly what it describes in each occurrence.

This Greek LXX verb means “battle”: to engage in armed conflict or fight against an opponent. It is a verb, so it describes the action of battling rather than a person, place, or object. The word occurs 199 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, showing that it is used broadly for military conflict. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This verb means “foresee” or “see previously.” It describes seeing something before a later moment, whether by anticipating it or by having seen it earlier. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, including three Old Testament passages and one passage in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains knowledge or sight that comes before the moment being discussed.

“Strain still more” means to apply additional force or effort after strain has already been applied. As a verb, it describes intensifying an existing exertion rather than beginning an entirely separate action. In the Greek LXX corpus, this word occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 9:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic sense is continued, increased straining.

This LXX word is a proper name, given as “Ptolemaΐs” or “Ptolemes.” It functions as a name rather than as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The precise person or place it identifies must be determined from the surrounding passage, which is not included here. It occurs 51 times in the Greek LXX corpus, especially in 1 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees.

Saphatia is a proper name, rendered as “Saphatia” or “Safatia.” It identifies people in the Greek Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs nine times across the LXX corpus, in 1 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. Because the available passages do not include their verse text or surrounding context, the name’s personal referent must be determined from each passage. Its basic meaning here is the personal name itself.

Semeias is a proper name, also rendered Semias. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs three times: once in Nehemiah and twice in Esther. The name appears in the books’ personal references, but the available wording does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the identity or role of each person named. Its basic meaning is therefore the personal name Semeias, with Semias as another rendering.

This Greek LXX noun means “implement,” referring generally to an object or tool used for a particular task. It appears four times in the Old Testament portion of the Greek LXX, in Deuteronomy, 2 Kings, and Ecclesiastes. Its precise reference—such as the kind of implement intended—depends on the surrounding verse, since the word itself gives the general idea of a usable tool or object rather than naming one specific instrument.

Sokchōtha, also written Sokkhotha, is a proper name. It identifies a specific person, place, or other named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. This name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, once in Exodus 12:37 and once in Joshua 13:27. Without the surrounding verse text, the evidence here establishes the name’s form and use as a proper noun, but not which kind of named entity it identifies in each passage.

This adjective describes something uncommon or in short supply—something rare or scarce. It points to limited availability or unusual occurrence rather than naming a person, action, or specific object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Proverbs 32:17, so its exact force there must be understood from that passage’s wording and surrounding context. Its basic sense remains a description of something not often found or not plentiful.

This adjective describes something plaited or woven together, with separate strands or parts joined into one connected whole. It presents the idea of interweaving rather than merely placing things side by side. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Exodus 36:30, so its normal lexical sense is clear even though its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “join in supporting.” It describes taking part with others in giving strength, help, or reinforcement rather than acting alone. As a verb, it expresses supportive action—coming alongside someone or something to help it succeed or stand firm. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in 2 Chronicles and once in Esther. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and wider context.

Sōbak, also rendered Sovak, is a proper name referring to a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Samuel: 10:16 and 10:18. Because it is a personal name rather than a descriptive term, its basic meaning is the identification of the individual named Sōbak; the surrounding passage is needed to understand that person’s specific role in each reference.

This Greek LXX adjective means “quickest,” describing someone or something that acts, moves, or happens with greater speed than others. It expresses the highest degree of quickness rather than simply saying that something is quick. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 1:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains the superlative idea of being quickest.

This Greek LXX noun refers to punishment imposed in response to wrongdoing, including the idea of vengeance. It describes an act or measure of retribution rather than a person or quality. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, appearing in Proverbs, Jeremiah, Daniel, Wisdom, and the Maccabean writings. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense is corrective or retaliatory punishment.

This Greek LXX noun means nourishment or provisions—the food and supplies that sustain people. It can refer broadly to what is needed for life and daily support, rather than to a particular meal or kind of food. The word occurs 26 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, showing regular use for necessary sustenance. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the provision of food or support for living.

This adjective means “healthy”: sound in bodily condition rather than sick or diseased. In the LXX corpus, it occurs eight times, including several passages in Leviticus concerned with bodily condition. It can describe a person or condition that is well and sound. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains physical health and soundness. The word is also used in Joshua, Isaiah, and Sirach, showing its normal use across different settings.

This verb means “overlook”: to pass over something without giving it attention or consideration. In the Greek Old Testament, it can describe failing to notice a person or matter, or choosing not to take account of it. The word occurs 31 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages in Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Esther, Psalms, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

Phalet, also rendered Falet, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 2:47. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, the name itself does not support a further meaning beyond identifying the individual it names. Its normal function is simply personal identification.

Phanouēl, also rendered Fanoil, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person named Phanouēl. The name occurs six times across five verses, chiefly in Judges, with additional occurrences in 1 Kings and 1 Chronicles. Because it functions as a personal name, its meaning is primarily its identification of that individual; the surrounding verse is needed to understand what is said about him or the place associated with the name.

This Greek Old Testament verb means to spare someone or something, or to refrain from an action. It describes holding back rather than proceeding with what might otherwise be done. The word occurs 86 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing repeated use for deliberate restraint or mercy. Its basic sense remains the same whether the subject refrains from harming, avoids taking something, or withholds an action. The precise force in any particular verse depends on what the surrounding passage says is being withheld or avoided.

Chabasin is a proper name, rendered also as Khavasin. It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it identifies a particular named person or place in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Jeremiah 42:3. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific identity cannot be clarified further, but its basic function is that of a name rather than an ordinary descriptive word.

Chenara, also rendered Khenara, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Numbers 34:11. Because it functions as a name, its meaning is primarily its identification of a particular place or named entity, not a general concept that can be translated into an ordinary English definition.

Ōphir is a proper name, functioning as the name “Ōphir” or “Ofir.” It does not describe an action, quality, or ordinary object, but identifies what is named by this title. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears twice, both times in Job. These occurrences are found in Job 22:24 and Job 28:16. The precise significance of the name in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical meaning remains the proper name “Ōphir; Ofir.”
